name: Calibration and validation practice for traffic microsimulation (FHWA Toolbox Vol. III, UK TAG M3.1 / GEH, Indian Vissim and SUMO studies, data-free verification)
maintainer: US FHWA (Traffic Analysis Toolbox Vol. III: Dowling et al. 2004, FHWA-HRT-04-040; 2019 update FHWA-HOP-18-036); UK Department for Transport (TAG Unit M3.1, which absorbed the older DMRB Vol. 12 criteria; TfL modelling guidance is referenced for saturation flow); Indian academic groups (IIT Bombay, IIT Madras, IIT Kharagpur and others) for Vissim and SUMO calibration studies.
first_release: FHWA Toolbox Vol. III 2004; FHWA update 2019; GEH and flow criteria in UK DMRB Vol. 12 from 1996 [uncertain] and now in TAG M3.1 (version read: May 2026).
last_activity: TAG M3.1 PDF dated May 2026; TxDOT microsimulation chapter applying FHWA 2004 and 2019 criteria, current.
licence: Public government guidance (FHWA public domain; UK Open Government Licence [uncertain]).
code_availability: Guidance documents only. Tooling that implements the multi-seed practice: SUMO runSeeds.py.
maintenance_health: FHWA moved in 2019 from fixed percentage targets to statistically derived bands (2-sigma and 1-sigma bands, bounded dynamic absolute and systematic error). TAG M3.1 is revised regularly and keeps the GEH and 15% criteria.
known_limitations: 1) STANDARD CRITERIA. FHWA Toolbox Vol. III (2004), Table 4 (Wisconsin DOT freeway criteria). Individual link hourly flows must be within 100 veh/h when the flow is under 700 veh/h, within 15% for 700-2700 veh/h, and within 400 veh/h above 2700 veh/h, each in more than 85% of cases. The sum of all link flows must be within 5% of the sum of counts. GEH must be below 5 for individual link flows in more than 85% of cases, and below 4 for the sum of all links. Journey times must be within 15% (or 1 min, whichever is higher) in more than 85% of cases. Visual audits of speed-flow and queuing are accepted to the analyst's satisfaction. The recommended order is capacity calibration first, then route choice, then system performance. FHWA 2019 (FHWA-HOP-18-036 ch. 5), with all four criteria met in a single run per travel condition: I) 95% of simulated outputs inside the ~2-sigma band of the representative day, with one exception allowed if there are fewer than 20 intervals; II) two-thirds inside the 1-sigma band, including two non-adjacent critical intervals; III) mean absolute error at or below the bounded dynamic absolute error threshold; IV) absolute mean signed error at or below one third of that threshold. Use one real representative day, not a synthetic average, and at least two measures (a travel time or speed profile plus a bottleneck measure). UK TAG M3.1 Table 2 uses the same flow bands (100 veh/h / 15% / 400 veh/h) and GEH below 5 in more than 85% of cases. Table 1 requires screenlines within 5% in about 95% of cases. Table 3 requires journey times within 15% (or 1 min if higher) on more than 85% of routes. Appendix C for microsimulation adds: exit flows GEH below 5 on at least 85%; turning movements meeting both criteria on at least 85% and practitioners usually requiring all GEH below 10; journey times within 15% AND within 60 s; queue profiles compared every 5 minutes or so; saturation flow validation following TfL guidance. GEH = sqrt(2 (M - C)^2 / (M + C)), with M the modelled and C the observed hourly flow. TxDOT reads GEH below 3 as a good fit, 3-5 as acceptable for local roads only, and above 5 as unacceptable. 2) REPLICATIONS. FHWA 2004 Appendix B: the confidence interval is 2 t(1-alpha/2, N-1) s / sqrt(N). Table 8 gives minimum runs for a desired CI/s at 95% confidence: 83 for 0.5, 23 for 1.0, 12 for 1.5 and 8 for 2.0. Example: delay SD of 1.5 s and a desired CI of 3.0 s needs 8 runs. To tell two alternatives apart, Appendix E (Eq. 17) needs 4 runs per alternative when the difference to detect is 2 pooled SDs. TAG C.3.13-C.3.14 asks for multiple seeds, reported confidence intervals and enough runs that alternatives can be told apart, and forbids cherry-picking single runs for visuals. FHWA 2019 says calibration is done on one run per condition, and that if seeds change results significantly, check for coding errors or gridlock. SUMO is deterministic for a fixed seed (default 23423); --random breaks reproducibility; runSeeds.py repeats runs over many seeds. 3) INDIAN STUDIES. Mathew and Radhakrishnan (2010, ASCE J. Urban Planning and Development): Vissim at signalized intersections in two Indian cities; parameters picked by sensitivity analysis, then a genetic algorithm minimising the field-simulated delay error. Manjunatha, Vortisch and Mathew (TRB 2013): Mumbai signalized intersections; Latin hypercube sampling plus GA; Wiedemann 74 and 99; five parameters chosen by two-way ANOVA; delay as the measure of effectiveness. Maheshwary et al. (2020): Kolkata corridor; class-specific Vissim parameters by GA; travel time as the measure; the optimum values differed significantly between vehicle classes at 95% confidence. Sashank et al. (2020, RATE 2018 proceedings): SUMO on a 2 km Chennai segment; 14 sensitive parameters found by one-way ANOVA, then optimised by trial and error and by GA; average speeds compared with MAPE against field data and against calibrated Vissim, with comparable results (exact MAPE not retrieved [uncertain]). Mer et al. (2022): 7 intersections; 11 of 19 Vissim parameters found sensitive and calibrated with a Python GA (GEATPy). Chaudhari et al. (2021): Wiedemann-99 calibrated on trajectories by RMSE. Kulkarni, Chaudhari et al. (2024, Chennai trajectories): 70/30 estimation and holdout split of leader-follower pairs (436 / 187); holdout position RMSE about 7 m for the best method [uncertain exact value]. Lateral clearance parameters by class and Wiedemann CC0/CC1-type headway parameters are the usual tuning targets [uncertain for the specific parameter names in each paper]. The typical Indian pattern is sensitivity screening, then GA optimisation, with a single macroscopic measure (delay, travel time or speed) at one or a few sites.
documented_failures: a) Fit-equals-validation: many studies tune parameters by GA on the same delay or travel-time data they then report as validation. TAG asks for data used in calibration and independent validation data to be reported separately, and says meeting the targets does not prove fitness for purpose. b) Non-transferability: Maheshwary et al. found class-dependent optima and recommended recalibration elsewhere; Prabhash and Amarasingha (Colombo) and Mer et al. warned that their parameters hold only for similar sites. c) Over-parameterisation: FHWA 2019 warns that more adjustable parameters give more freedom to fit one day, so the adjustable set should be kept small. d) Smoothing the target: averaging several days gives unrealistically smooth measures that a model cannot and should not reproduce (FHWA 2019). e) Single-run visuals: TAG C.3.13 warns against cherry-picked runs. f) Seed instability hiding bugs: FHWA 2019 says large differences between seeds point to coding errors or gridlock, not to natural variability. g) GEH on tiny flows: Dhaka and Chennai junction studies report GEH below 5 on 6 exits from 37 of 500 parameter combinations; many combinations pass, so passing GEH alone does not identify the parameters (ICCESD 2024 study).
validation_approach: TIER 0, verification without field data (all achievable in 72 hours, all automatable as tests): (1) Vehicle conservation per class and per link: vehicles entered = exited + present + explicitly removed, every step, and removals (teleports or deadlock clears) counted and shown. (2) No overlaps or collisions: no vehicle footprint intersects another, speeds never negative, accelerations within class bounds. (3) Fundamental diagram shape on a ring road or long straight link: the free-flow branch slope matches the desired speed v0; flow peaks then falls; the jam end approaches 1/(s0 + l) per class for single-class runs; for mixed runs, express density as area occupancy. (4) Capacity versus road width: capacity rises monotonically with carriageway width, and per-lane-equivalent values fall in a stated band around Indo-HCM (about 1200-2000 PCU/h/lane urban; saturation flow about 1140 - 60 W PCU/h per metre for 7-10.5 m approaches). (5) Determinism: same seed, scenario and timestep give a bit-identical state hash after N steps, on the same browser and on a second browser; use a seeded PRNG only, never Math.random, and a fixed timestep. (6) Timestep convergence: halving dt changes headline outputs by less than a stated tolerance. (7) Replications: run at least 5-10 seeds per scenario and report the mean with a 95% CI; use FHWA Table 8 to justify the count (e.g. CI/s = 2 at 95% needs 8 runs) and 4 runs per alternative to detect a 2-SD difference. (8) Scenario sanity: closing a lane lowers capacity; a red signal stops discharge; adding a flyover removes conflict delay. TIER 1, plausibility against published numbers: Indo-HCM capacities and saturation flow, and the Chennai Saidapet per-class speeds (cars 6.13, motorcycles 6.01, heavy 5.64, autos 5.06 m/s) on a 245 m x 11.2 m replay. TIER 2, calibration and validation to FHWA / TAG standards: needs site-specific counts, journey times and queues, which a 72-hour build does not have.
takeaway_for_our_build: Claim only what the evidence supports, and say it in the UI and README. A 72-hour build can credibly claim: 'verified' (Tier 0 tests pass in CI, with results published); 'plausible against Indian references' (capacity within X% of Indo-HCM for given widths, saturation flow within Y% of 1140 - 60 W, Chennai per-class mean speeds within Z%), with the tolerances stated beforehand; and 'stochastic results reported as mean +- 95% CI over N seeds'. It must NOT claim 'calibrated', 'validated', 'meets GEH/FHWA criteria', or accurate absolute delay, emissions or safety for a real junction. Those need site counts, a holdout dataset and the FHWA 2019 or TAG procedure. Design rules: (1) seeded PRNG plus fixed dt plus a state-hash test from day one; (2) a conservation counter and a deadlock or teleport counter shown in the results panel; (3) a built-in GEH and percentage-error calculator so users with their own counts can calibrate later, with the TAG thresholds (GEH below 5 on at least 85% of links, journey times within 15% and 60 s) shown as targets, not as achieved; (4) keep the user-tunable parameter set small (desired speed, time gap, minimum gap, lateral clearance per class); (5) results compare alternatives against each other under identical seeds rather than presenting absolute numbers as forecasts; (6) every chart shows how many seeds were run and the CI band, and never a single cherry-picked run.
